Its tone has a metallic quality and a wide range, from a deep resonance to a high, sharp sound. The instrument resonates when its body is struck directly, and the sound carries well. The sansi's colour is bright and transparent, like the high frequencies of a xylophone or a metallophone, but with a warmth of its own. Its resonance depends on the vibration of the body itself and produces long, rich overtones. Compared with drums it is clearer and more definitely pitched; compared with strings it has a more direct impact and an instant burst of sound.

The sansi and the mbira are alternative names or variants of the same thing, also called the kalimba or thumb piano. It is the traditional instrument of the Shona in Malawi and Zimbabwe in Africa, a lamellophone and a plucked idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 122.1. It consists of a wooden board, often with a resonator, carrying staggered metal tongues; the player holds it with both hands and plucks the tongues with thumb and index finger. Eastern and southern Africa have several instruments of this kind, often played together with hosho percussion, and used at religious ceremonies, weddings and other social gatherings. In 2020 the craft of making and playing the mbira/sansi in Malawi and Zimbabwe was inscribed on the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage.
桑西琴／姆比拉家族的基本構造為木製琴板，其上裝有錯落排列的金屬彈片（簧片），演奏: The basic construction of the sansi/mbira family is a wooden board fitted with staggered metal tongues (reeds), plucked with the thumb or a finger. The sources note that the tongues were originally bamboo and later became metal keys; the board often has a resonator, but its material is not recorded. Apart from the wooden board and the bamboo or metal tongues, the sources say nothing about the fittings, the resonator box or the decorative materials.

舌片琴屬撥奏體鳴，在非洲存在數千年。西非約三千年前有木竹舌片，尚比西河谷約一千三: The lamellophone is a plucked idiophone that has existed in Africa for thousands of years. West Africa had wooden and bamboo tongues about three thousand years ago, metal tongues appeared in the Zambezi valley about 1,300 years ago and later spread across the continent, and types and uses diverged among the Shona of Zimbabwe and in Mozambique. In the 1950s Hugh Tracey designed the kalimba on the model of the mbira nyunga nyunga and put it into production; in the 1960s and early 1970s Maurice White, Thomas Mapfumo and others brought it to the modern stage. In 2020 the craft of making and playing the mbira/sansi in Malawi and Zimbabwe was inscribed on the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage.
